study_title: Developmental outcomes of 3,4-methylenedioxymethamphetamine (ecstasy)-exposed infants in the UK.
authors: Lynn T. Singer; Derek G. Moore; Meeyoung O. Min; Julia Goodwin; John Turner; Sarah Fulton; A. C. Parrott
publication_type: Journal Article | Research Support, N.I.H., Extramural
funders: National Institute on Drug Abuse | NIDA NIH HHS
condition_or_population: Infant developmental outcomes following prenatal MDMA exposure
population_or_subgroup: Infants prenatally exposed to MDMA; heavier- and lighter-exposure groups compared with non-MDMA-exposed infants
comparator: Non-MDMA-exposed infants; lighter-exposure infants compared with heavier-exposure infants
dose_or_regimen: Maternal self-reported recreational use during pregnancy; exposure groups were defined by a median split of total tablets averaged over pregnancy. Heavier users averaged 1.3 (1.4) tablets versus 0.07 (0.04) for lighter users; only one woman reported use in the third trimester.
sample_size: 96 infants: 28 MDMA-exposed (13 heavier, 15 lighter) and 68 non-MDMA-exposed
outcome_measure: Bayley Psychomotor Development Index (PDI), Alberta Infant Motor Scales (AIMS), and examiner-rated Behavioral Rating Scales (BRS) motor measures
clinical_endpoint: Fine and gross motor development and motor delays
assessment_timepoint: 4, 12, 18, and 24 months; AIMS and BRS motor findings at 4 months, and PDI and BRS motor findings at 12 months
effect_or_statistic: At 4 months, AIMS mean percentiles were 35.1 ± 24 in the heavier-exposure group, 65.7 ± 23 in the lighter-exposure group, and 45.9 ± 28 in the nonexposed group (p < 0.03). At 12 months, PDI means were 76 ± 12 for heavier exposure, 99.8 ± 12 for lighter exposure, and 92.0 ± 16 for no exposure (F = 10.7, p < 0.002). Longitudinal motor effect: PDI = 90.8 (SE = 3.8) for heavier exposure versus 98.7 (SE = 1.4) for lighter and nonexposed children.
finding_summary: Prenatal MDMA exposure, particularly heavier exposure, was associated with poorer infant motor performance. Motor differences were reported at 4 and 12 months, and longitudinal analyses found a main effect of MDMA exposure on motor outcomes through assessments from 4 to 24 months. The abstract characterized motor delays as evident at each age.
study_design: Prospective longitudinal cohort following infants from birth to 2 years, with two-group and three-group comparisons and mixed linear models controlling for covariates.
support: Prenatal MDMA exposure, particularly heavier exposure, was associated with poorer infant motor performance. Motor differences were reported at 4 and 12 months, and longitudinal analyses found a main effect of MDMA exposure on motor outcomes through assessments from 4 to 24 months. The abstract characterized motor delays as evident at each age.
